samples.narration: Aircraft rumble fades, but someone is still talking. Active noise cancellation works on pressure at your ear, not sound categories.
Outside noise reaches the ear through one path. The headphone speaker adds another pressure contribution. What remains is their sum.
In this ideal single-tone model, matching amplitude and opposite phase at the target makes the residual shrink to zero.
Now keep the amplitude and shift the control wave. The residual returns because the peaks and troughs no longer match.
Assume a timing error of one tenth of a millisecond: three point six degrees at one hundred hertz, but thirty-six at one thousand.
This tightens timing tolerance, not a universal frequency wall. Reference preview, acoustic paths, bandwidth, and feedback stability also matter.
Passive isolation changes transmission through the seal and ear cup. Active control adds pressure. Switching it off leaves the barrier in place.
Speech is not one high-frequency tone. Some components can be reduced while enough residual survives for the voice to remain audible.
Here is a counterexample: active control can reduce low-frequency amplification of your own voice caused by a closed ear canal.
That does not promise to erase another person's whole voice. More noticeable speech does not prove its pressure was amplified.
Also check the mode. Transparency deliberately lets outside sound in, while adaptive modes can change the balance on supported devices.
Fit changes acoustic paths too. Compare cancellation on and off without moving the headphones or changing the source.
Published prototype measurements varied with wearer and fit. We ran no acoustic test, and this model cannot predict your personal reduction.
Ask what remains at the ear: path, timing, fit, and mode. Audible speech can still be attenuated.
